highlights.idea: Ordinary perception during earthly life discloses only the dense aspect of creatures.
highlights.teaching: The dense-aspect claim is explained as a limit on access, in the visible–invisible argument.

highlights.idea: Supersensible recognition requires insight and understanding; the sentence continues beyond the highlight.
highlights.teaching: The continuation and preceding death/rebirth passage explain the condition and purpose of recognition.

highlights.idea: The deer is oriented toward the cosmic surroundings rather than chiefly toward Earth.
highlights.teaching: The orientation supplies the premise for selecting a deer organ rather than an arbitrary container.
The explanation returns to the horn/antler distinction in Agriculture I, pages 83–84.

highlights.idea: A kidney–bladder process is said to preserve the activity associated with yarrow.
highlights.teaching: The organ process links the plant’s sulfur relationship to the proposed sheath.

highlights.idea: The bladder’s material constitution matters to that process.
highlights.teaching: The organ is treated as an active participant, not merely a storage bag.

highlights.idea: Thin material can embody extensive forces: the bladder as a cosmic replica.
highlights.teaching: The substance/force distinction explains the comparison, with the lack of a demonstrated mechanism made explicit.

highlights.idea: Yarrow is associated primarily with potash activity.
highlights.teaching: Yarrow’s sulfur/potassium role is compared directly with the chamomile role.

highlights.idea: Drawing in calcium as well requires another plant.
highlights.teaching: The surrounding text identifies chamomile and explains the added calcium relation and intestinal sheath.

highlights.idea: Mercury, Venus and Moon influences pass through soil and support reproductive succession.
highlights.teaching: The editor’s synopsis is distinguished from the lecture; pages 115–117 explain the soil/lime route and seed succession.

highlights.idea: Jupiter, Mars and Saturn influences support fruiting.
highlights.teaching: Fruiting is unpacked through the following distinction between edible expansion and propagation, with the silica relationship explained.

limits: All 135 capture pages have an inventory entry and teaching commentary. Every identified highlighted idea has a dedicated explanation and an audit link. Page coverage does not mean every printed sentence is reproduced.

Figure 7’s conceptual structure and the dates discussed in the surrounding prose are taught. A reliable transcription and independent reconciliation of every small handwritten date and alternative layer label in that diagram remains deferred; no such details have been guessed.

The bibliography is covered as a reading map. The contents of all its listed books, and the complete source works behind Courtney’s nested citations, have not been independently read or verified in this task.
The full GA 136, GA 230 and GA 327 cycles are outside this anthology. Later orchard, vineyard, livestock and other discussions promised within the original courses are not silently reconstructed.
The scientific comparisons address specific disagreements. They are not a systematic review of all biodynamic farming trials, preparation efficacy or calendar research.
The new detailed companion is in English. The existing nine-lesson course remains available in English and Brazilian Portuguese; a complete Portuguese translation of this expansion is not included.
Page references are PDF captures. The Kindle locations recorded for highlights identify the displayed capture start, not the exact beginning of each highlighted sentence.

The PDF contains flattened page images and no PDF annotation objects. Four visible yellow highlight passages were identified by screening all 135 extracted images and inspecting the candidates at full size. Marks absent from this supplied capture cannot be audited.
